Appendix A Wyner-Ziv Corollaries

Corollary 36 (Benchmark Gap Closure).

Under the one-way reduction (Proposition 25), the converse and pipelined achievability are governed by the same WZ benchmark. For i.i.d. blocks drawn from the stationary marginal p⁡(qA)p(q_{A}), the WZ single-letter formula applies:

RWZ(D)=minp⁡(u∣qA):𝔼⁡[dintent]≤D[I(QA;U)−I(QB;U)],R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D)\;=\;\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}p(u\mid q_{A}):\\ \mathbb{E}[d_{\mathrm{intent}}]\leq D\end{subarray}}\bigl[I(Q_{A};\,U)-I(Q_{B};\,U)\bigr],

where UU forms the Markov chain QB→QA→UQ_{B}\to Q_{A}\to U. This formula is exact for the i.i.d. source; for the ergodic Markov quotient process, the same objective serves as a conservative constructive upper bound when we restrict attention to memoryless auxiliaries UU and ignore temporal correlation.

Corollary 37 (Inherited Results).

Under the conditions of Proposition 25, the semantic setting inherits strong converses [29] (distortion approaches dmaxd_{\max} exponentially below Rsem​(D)R_{\mathrm{sem}}(D)), error exponents [29] matching the WZ reliability function, and finite-blocklength bounds [30] (R⁡(n,D,ε)=Rsem​(D)+V/n​Q−1​(ε)+O⁡(log⁡n/n)R(n,D,\varepsilon)=R_{\mathrm{sem}}(D)+\sqrt{V/n}\,Q^{-1}(\varepsilon)+O(\log n/n)).

Appendix B Claim / Validation Ledger

Appendix C Quotient Facts Used in This Paper

This paper does not re-prove the full Myhill–Nerode theorem of [4]. The later sections use only three structural facts: right-invariance of the history equivalence, refinement monotonicity as capacity increases, and the resulting canonical coarsening map 𝒬A→𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{A}\to\mathcal{Q}_{B}. We collect those facts here so the notation used in the rate-distortion arguments is self-contained. Uniqueness and minimality of the quotient remain imported background from [4].

Lemma 38 (Right-invariance and well-defined quotient transitions).

If h≡m,Th′h\equiv_{m,T}h^{\prime}, then for every observation o∈𝒪o\in\mathcal{O}, the extended histories satisfy ho≡m,Th′oho\equiv_{m,T}h^{\prime}o. Consequently the transition [h]→𝑜[h​o][h]\xrightarrow{o}[ho] is independent of the chosen representative.

Proof.

If h≡m,Th′h\equiv_{m,T}h^{\prime}, then every controller π∈Πm,T\pi\in\Pi_{m,T} induces the same future observation law from hh and h′h^{\prime}. Conditioning both laws on one additional observation oo preserves equality by the chain rule for conditional distributions in the finite POMDP, so ho≡m,Th′oho\equiv_{m,T}h^{\prime}o. The quotient transition therefore depends only on the class [h][h], not on the representative history. ∎

Lemma 39 (Refinement monotonicity in capacity).

If mA≥mBm_{A}\geq m_{B} and TA=TB=TT_{A}=T_{B}=T, then 𝒬A⪯𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{A}\preceq\mathcal{Q}_{B}.

Proof.

Since mA≥mBm_{A}\geq m_{B}, every FSC with at most mBm_{B} nodes is also an FSC with at most mAm_{A} nodes, so ΠmB,T⊆ΠmA,T\Pi_{m_{B},T}\subseteq\Pi_{m_{A},T}. Therefore equality of future observation laws against all controllers in ΠmA,T\Pi_{m_{A},T} implies equality against all controllers in ΠmB,T\Pi_{m_{B},T}. Hence h≡mA,Th′h\equiv_{m_{A},T}h^{\prime} implies h≡mB,Th′h\equiv_{m_{B},T}h^{\prime}, so every 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-class is contained in a unique 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class. ∎

Proposition 40 (Canonical coarsening map).

Under the conditions of Lemma 39, the map

κA→B:𝒬A→𝒬B,κA→B​([h]A):=[h]B,\kappa_{A\to B}:\mathcal{Q}_{A}\to\mathcal{Q}_{B},\qquad\kappa_{A\to B}([h]_{A}):=[h]_{B},

is well-defined. It is surjective onto the reachable 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-classes.

Proof.

Well-definedness follows from Lemma 39: if [h]A=[h′]A[h]_{A}=[h^{\prime}]_{A}, then h≡mA,Th′h\equiv_{m_{A},T}h^{\prime}, hence h≡mB,Th′h\equiv_{m_{B},T}h^{\prime} and therefore [h]B=[h′]B[h]_{B}=[h^{\prime}]_{B}. Surjectivity onto reachable 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-classes is immediate because each reachable 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class contains at least one history hh, and that history belongs to some 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-class whose image under κA→B\kappa_{A\to B} is exactly [h]B[h]_{B}. ∎

Appendix D Extended Capacity Theorem Remarks

Remark 41 (Positivity of cMc_{M}).

cM>0c_{M}>0 whenever 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} is strictly finer than 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}, as a consequence of the definitions. In a finite POMDP, the posterior belief bh=P⁡(st∣ht)b_{h}=P(s_{t}\mid h_{t}) is a sufficient statistic for the future observation distribution under any policy [4]: PMπ(𝒪t+1:T∣h)P_{M}^{\pi}(\mathcal{O}_{t+1:T}\mid h) depends on hh only through bhb_{h}. Hence if bh=bh′b_{h}=b_{h^{\prime}}, then hh and h′h^{\prime} produce identical future observations under all policies—including all FSCs in ΠmA,TA\Pi_{m_{A},T_{A}}—and therefore lie in the same quotient class. Contrapositively, if [h]A≠[h′]A[h]_{A}\neq[h^{\prime}]_{A}, then bh≠bh′b_{h}\neq b_{h^{\prime}}. Since 𝒲1​(b,b′)>0\mathcal{W}_{1}(b,b^{\prime})>0 for distinct distributions on a finite state space, the belief component of dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}} is strictly positive: dintent​(IntentA​(h),IntentA​(h′))≥𝒲1​(bh,bh′)>0d_{\mathrm{intent}}(\mathrm{Intent}_{A}(h),\mathrm{Intent}_{A}(h^{\prime}))\geq\mathcal{W}_{1}(b_{h},b_{h^{\prime}})>0. Finiteness of 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} and 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B} then gives cM≥min[h]A≠[h′]A⁡𝒲1​(bh,bh′)>0c_{M}\geq\min_{[h]_{A}\neq[h^{\prime}]_{A}}\mathcal{W}_{1}(b_{h},b_{h^{\prime}})>0.

Remark 42 (Positive-support condition in Theorem 18(i)).

The impossibility proof needs one additional condition beyond strict refinement: at least one merged 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class witnessing the pigeonhole argument must appear with positive stationary mass under the protocol-induced source law. In finite irreducible settings this is automatic for every reachable recurrent class; we state it explicitly because mere convergence to stationarity does not by itself guarantee positive mass on every merged class.

Role of BB’s quotient.

BB’s computational bound (mBm_{B}-node FSC) means its effective information state at each step is its 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class. The quotient theorem [4] establishes that 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B} is the unique minimal abstraction preserving observation laws for all policies in ΠmB,TB\Pi_{m_{B},T_{B}}. Since BB’s policy is constrained to this class, two histories in the same 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class produce identical conditional observation distributions under any policy BB can execute. Messages from AA allow BB to reconfigure its FSC parameters—selecting which mBm_{B}-node policy to run—but not to transcend the mBm_{B} memory bound. The impossibility below RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}} arises because BB’s bounded processing cannot resolve the relevant 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses, even with optimal use of received messages.

Interpretation: structural impossibility.

The existence of a phase transition is a structural consequence of the quotient refinement 𝒬A⪯𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{A}\preceq\mathcal{Q}_{B}, which is policy-independent once the common-history comparison regime is fixed. When 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} is strictly finer than 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}, certain distinctions that AA can perceive are invisible to BB regardless of the protocol. The location of the most informative benchmark (Rcrit=h¯​(QA∣QB)R_{\mathrm{crit}}=\bar{h}(Q_{A}\mid Q_{B}) under Proposition 25) depends on the source distribution; the log-cardinality form provides a policy-independent worst-case reference, while theorem-level exponential achievability is claimed only in the one-way memoryless regime of Theorem 18(ii).

Appendix E Extended Converse Remarks

Remark 43 (Entropy rate and tightness).

Let hA:=limT→∞1T​H​(QAT)h_{A}:=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}H(Q_{A}^{T}) and hB:=limT→∞1T​H​(QBT)h_{B}:=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}H(Q_{B}^{T}) denote the entropy rates of the quotient processes, which exist under Assumption 19. The shrinking-distortion converse (Theorem 20) depends on hA−hBh_{A}-h_{B}. The benchmark is closest to the log-cardinality reference when the quotient processes have near-maximal entropy (hA≈log⁡|𝒬A|h_{A}\approx\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|, hB≈log⁡|𝒬B|h_{B}\approx\log|\mathcal{Q}_{B}|), i.e. under approximately uniform visitation of quotient classes.

Appendix F Full Wyner-Ziv Reduction Proof

This appendix provides the detailed proof of Proposition 25 (one-way Wyner-Ziv reduction).

Proof of Proposition 25.

The proof proceeds in four steps; Steps 1–2 are definitional, Step 3 is the main technical content, and Step 4 follows from [29].

Step 1 (Source identification). Under Assumptions 14, 19, and 23, the quotient process {QtA}t≥1\{Q_{t}^{A}\}_{t\geq 1} induced by the common history source is stationary and ergodic on the finite alphabet 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}. Because BB’s actions do not feed back into the sender-side source history, {QtA}\{Q_{t}^{A}\} is a well-defined source independent of the decoder.

Step 2 (Side information identification). Since 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} and 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B} are both defined on that same history space, Proposition 40 gives a canonical map κA→B:𝒬A→𝒬B\kappa_{A\to B}\colon\mathcal{Q}_{A}\to\mathcal{Q}_{B} with QBT=κA→B​(QAT)Q_{B}^{T}=\kappa_{A\to B}(Q_{A}^{T}) pointwise. Thus QBTQ_{B}^{T} serves as decoder side information correlated with the source QATQ_{A}^{T}. We do not claim this deterministic coarsening step for a genuinely distinct-sensor model unless it is first reduced to the same common-history setting.

Step 3 (Achievability: exact i.i.d., argued ergodic). Any Wyner-Ziv code for the source QATQ_{A}^{T} with decoder side information QBTQ_{B}^{T} at distortion DD under dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}} operates at rate RWZ​(D)R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D). By Assumption 15, dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}} is well-defined as a function of quotient class pairs (qA,q^A)∈𝒬A×𝒬A(q_{A},\hat{q}_{A})\in\mathcal{Q}_{A}\times\mathcal{Q}_{A}, so the WZ distortion matrix is unambiguous. Such a code can be implemented as a semantic communication protocol as follows.

Causal pipeline construction. The protocol of Definition 13 requires BB to act at every step, while WZ coding is block-based at blocklength nn. We bridge this gap with a pipelined scheme that respects causality. Divide time into blocks of nn steps. During block kk, AA accumulates quotient classes QA(k):=(Q(k−1)​n+1A,…,Qk​nA)Q_{A}^{(k)}:=(Q_{(k-1)n+1}^{A},\ldots,Q_{kn}^{A}) and simultaneously transmits the WZ codeword for the previous block QA(k−1)Q_{A}^{(k-1)} at rate RR bits/step. Upon receiving the codeword at the end of block kk, BB decodes Q^A(k−1)\hat{Q}_{A}^{(k-1)} and uses it to select FSC parameters θ(k+1)\theta^{(k+1)} for block k+1k+1. During block 1 (before any codeword is available), BB runs a default FSC θ0\theta_{0}; the resulting distortion D0≤dmaxD_{0}\leq d_{\max} is bounded. Over KK blocks, the average distortion is

D¯K=D0+(K−1)​DWZK→K→∞DWZ≤D,\bar{D}_{K}=\frac{D_{0}+(K-1)D_{\mathrm{WZ}}}{K}\;\xrightarrow{K\to\infty}\;D_{\mathrm{WZ}}\leq D,

so the pipeline overhead vanishes asymptotically. The per-step rate remains RR; the cost is a one-block decoding delay, which is standard in block coding [18].

From WZ reconstruction to semantic distortion. The standard WZ achievability theorem for stationary ergodic sources [29] guarantees the existence of a block code at rate RWZ​(D)R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D) whose time-averaged reconstruction distortion converges to ≤D\leq D as blocklength n→∞n\to\infty. The pipeline applies this code to successive blocks: during block k+1k{+}1, BB runs an FSC with parameters θ(k+1)\theta^{(k+1)} chosen from the decoded block k−1k{-}1.

I.I.D. case (exact). When the quotient source is memoryless (i.i.d. blocks), the parameter θ(k+1)=f⁡(Q^A(k−1),QB(k−1))\theta^{(k+1)}=f(\hat{Q}_{A}^{(k-1)},Q_{B}^{(k-1)}) is independent of QA(k+1)Q_{A}^{(k+1)}, and each block’s distortion equals DWZD_{\mathrm{WZ}} exactly. No mixing argument is needed, and the pipeline achieves the WZ rate-distortion function with equality: Rsem​(D)=RWZ​(D)R_{\mathrm{sem}}(D)=R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D). This proves Corollary 26.

Ergodic case (argued with mixing bounds). For a correlated ergodic source, the per-block distortion may fluctuate because θ(k+1)=f⁡(Q^A(k−1),QB(k−1))\theta^{(k+1)}=f(\hat{Q}_{A}^{(k-1)},Q_{B}^{(k-1)}) is correlated with QA(k+1)Q_{A}^{(k+1)} through the source dependence. Under Assumption 19, the quotient process on a finite state space has a unique stationary distribution and exhibits geometric mixing: ∥ℙ(QtA∈⋅∣Q0A=q)−μ∥TV≤C0ρt\|\mathbb{P}(Q_{t}^{A}\in\cdot\mid Q_{0}^{A}=q)-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq C_{0}\rho^{t} for some ρ<1\rho<1 and C0>0C_{0}>0. The two-block delay in the pipeline creates a gap of 2​n2n steps between the data used to select θ(k+1)\theta^{(k+1)} and the block QA(k+1)Q_{A}^{(k+1)} it governs. The correlation between these decays as C0​ρ2​nC_{0}\rho^{2n}. For any target tolerance δ>0\delta>0, choosing blocklength

n≥2​log⁡(C0/δ)log⁡(1/ρ)n\;\geq\;\frac{2\log(C_{0}/\delta)}{\log(1/\rho)}

ensures the per-block distortion deviation from DWZD_{\mathrm{WZ}} is at most δ\delta. Combined with the ergodic theorem applied to the joint process (QA(k),Q^A(k))(Q_{A}^{(k)},\hat{Q}_{A}^{(k)}), the time-averaged semantic distortion 1K​∑k=1Kdintent(k)\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}d_{\mathrm{intent}}^{(k)} converges almost surely to 𝔼⁡[dintent​(QA,Q^A)]≤D\mathbb{E}[d_{\mathrm{intent}}(Q_{A},\hat{Q}_{A})]\leq D. The pipeline overhead from block 1 vanishes as K→∞K\to\infty, yielding D¯K≤DWZ+δ+D0/K\bar{D}_{K}\leq D_{\mathrm{WZ}}+\delta+D_{0}/K. This supplies an asymptotic-average achievability bridge from WZ reconstruction distortion to semantic distortion. Upgrading to a blockwise identification would require an explicit coupling that we do not provide.

Parameter optimization. At the end of block kk, BB has decoded Q^A(k−1)\hat{Q}_{A}^{(k-1)} and observed QB(k−1)Q_{B}^{(k-1)}. It selects FSC parameters θ(k+1)\theta^{(k+1)} to minimize expected distortion given the decoded information: θ(k+1)=argminθ∈ΘmB𝔼[dintent∣Q^A(k−1),QB(k−1),θ]\theta^{(k+1)}=\arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta_{m_{B}}}\mathbb{E}[d_{\mathrm{intent}}\mid\hat{Q}_{A}^{(k-1)},Q_{B}^{(k-1)},\theta]. The parameter space ΘmB=Δ​(𝒜)mB×Δ​({1,…,mB})mB×|𝒪|\Theta_{m_{B}}=\Delta(\mathcal{A})^{m_{B}}\times\Delta(\{1,\ldots,m_{B}\})^{m_{B}\times|\mathcal{O}|} (Definition 13) is a product of simplices, hence compact. The expected distortion is continuous in θ\theta: the belief component bhBb_{h}^{B} and policy component πB(⋅|h)\pi_{B}(\cdot|h) are continuous functions of the FSC parameters (via the finite forward recursion), and dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}} is continuous in beliefs and policies. By the extreme value theorem, the minimum is attained. Since BB applies the optimized θ(k+1)\theta^{(k+1)} causally during block k+1k{+}1 (using only past decoded information), every action respects the protocol’s per-step structure.

Step 4 (Converse). Any semantic protocol (E,D)(E,D) at rate RR achieving Dintent≤DD_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq D induces a valid Wyner-Ziv code in this common-history coarsening setting: the message sequence MTM^{T} encodes QATQ_{A}^{T}, BB’s side information is QBT=κA→B​(QAT)Q_{B}^{T}=\kappa_{A\to B}(Q_{A}^{T}), and the achieved distortion DD is valid under dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}}. Since {QtA}\{Q_{t}^{A}\} is stationary ergodic (Step 1), the WZ converse for stationary ergodic sources [29] applies: R≥RWZ​(D)R\geq R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D).

Combining Steps 3–4 yields the benchmark identification. For i.i.d. sources, the identification is exact in both directions. For ergodic sources, the converse remains exact and the achievability is argued with explicit mixing-rate control; upgrading that final leg to an exact FSC-level pathwise identity remains open. ∎

Remark 44 (Conservative nature of the bound).

The conditional entropy rate h¯​(QA∣QB)\bar{h}(Q_{A}\mid Q_{B}) counts all distinctions visible to AA but not to BB. If some 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses are value-irrelevant (i.e., merging them does not change the optimal value), the true minimum rate could be lower. Formally, let QAvalQ_{A}^{\mathrm{val}} denote the coarsening of 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} retaining only value-relevant cells; then Hμ​(QAval∣QB)≤h¯​(QA∣QB)H_{\mu}(Q_{A}^{\mathrm{val}}\mid Q_{B})\leq\bar{h}(Q_{A}\mid Q_{B}), with equality when all 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-distinctions affect optimal value. This paper’s bounds are therefore conservative; tightening them to the value-relevant quotient is an open problem.

Appendix G Alignment Applications

This appendix provides extended discussion of alignment applications deferred from Section 9.

Model the human as agent HH with capacity (mH,TH)(m_{H},T_{H}) and the AI as agent AA with (mA,TA)≫(mH,TH)(m_{A},T_{A})\gg(m_{H},T_{H}).

RLHF.

In RLHF [46], human feedback provides ≈\approx1–2 bits per comparison (see footnote in §9). If the capacity mismatch maps to quotient structures, Corollary 35 predicts the scaling form Ncomparisons≥(log⁡|𝒬A|−log⁡|𝒬H|)/2+Ω⁡(log⁡(1/ε))N_{\mathrm{comparisons}}\geq(\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|-\log|\mathcal{Q}_{H}|)/2+\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon)): linear in the capacity gap, logarithmic in accuracy. This is a structural prediction about functional dependence, not a computable numerical bound—the precise quotient cardinalities |𝒬A||\mathcal{Q}_{A}|, |𝒬H||\mathcal{Q}_{H}| for LLM-scale systems remain unknown. Estimating effective quotient sizes from learned representations (e.g., via probing classifiers, the lattice-gradient approach of Appendix Q, or by identifying natural-language cross-probes that test whether a model distinguishes context AA from context BB) is the key open problem connecting this theory to practice.

Interpretability and debate.

Explanations are bandwidth-limited channels; the traversal theorem (Theorem 31) suggests routing through intermediate abstractions [12, 13]. Multiple debaters form a multi-access channel, increasing effective alignment bandwidth. By data processing, post-processing cannot improve alignment: Ralign(f(A)→H;ε)≥Ralign(A→H;ε)R_{\mathrm{align}}(f(A)\to H;\,\varepsilon)\geq R_{\mathrm{align}}(A\to H;\,\varepsilon); for intermediate agents: Ralign(A→H;ε)≤∑iRalign(Layeri→Layeri+1;ε/k)R_{\mathrm{align}}(A\to H;\,\varepsilon)\leq\sum_{i}R_{\mathrm{align}}(\mathrm{Layer}_{i}\to\mathrm{Layer}_{i+1};\,\varepsilon/k).

Connection to LLM routing (Appendix P).

The LLM routing experiment provides a concrete (if analogical) illustration of the phase transition in a practical setting. The 1-bit router operates at R=1R=1 bit/query. The framework predicts that routing quality depends on whether this rate exceeds RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}} for the effective quotient gap between the strong and weak models. The observation that single-token logprob routing fails on MMLU-Pro (APGR =0.457<=0.457< random =0.502=0.502) while self-consistency routing succeeds (APGR =2.216=2.216) is consistent with a phase transition: the logprob probe family induces a coarser effective quotient (fewer distinguishable difficulty classes), pushing RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}} above the 1-bit channel; the richer self-consistency probes yield a finer quotient, bringing RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}} below 1 bit. This illustrates how the theory’s qualitative predictions—that communication success depends on the interaction between channel capacity and the quotient structure induced by the probe family—manifest in practice.

Appendix H Proof of Theorem 18(i): Impossibility Below Critical Rate

Proof.

Fix a reachable 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class CkC_{k} with stationary mass π⁡(Ck)>0\pi(C_{k})>0 and rk>2Rr_{k}>2^{R} reachable 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses inside it. At rate RR, the encoder can produce at most 2R2^{R} messages per step. Since BB’s decoder is an mBm_{B}-node FSC (Definition 13), its effective per-step information state within the common-history comparison regime is the pair (received message, current 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class). Thus within CkC_{k} the decoder can distinguish at most 2R2^{R} of the rkr_{k} subclasses. By pigeonhole, at least one decoder state merges at least two reachable 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses inside CkC_{k}.

Conditional on visiting CkC_{k}, the probability of such a merge is at least 1−2R/rk1-2^{R}/r_{k}, so the unconditional confusion probability satisfies

pconfuse≥π⁡(Ck)​(1−2R/rk)> 0.p_{\mathrm{confuse}}\;\geq\;\pi(C_{k})\,\bigl(1-2^{R}/r_{k}\bigr)\;>\;0.

Whenever the decoder confuses two distinct merged 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses, the resulting intent distortion is at least cMc_{M} by definition. Therefore

Dintent≥pconfuse⋅cM> 0.∎D_{\mathrm{intent}}\;\geq\;p_{\mathrm{confuse}}\cdot c_{M}\;>\;0.\qed

Appendix I Proof of Theorem 18(ii): Constructive Decay in the One-Way Memoryless Regime

We prove the upper bound of Theorem 18(ii) only in the regime stated there: common-history coarsening, one-way observability, i.i.d. quotient source, and observation-Lipschitz reward. The proof imports the classical lossless WZ reliability exponent rather than deriving a new ambiguity-cell argument.

Assumption 45 (Observation-Lipschitz Reward).

The reward function is LRL_{R}-observation-Lipschitz: for all histories h,h′h,h^{\prime} and all π∈Πm,T\pi\in\Pi_{m,T}, |R¯(h,π)−R¯(h′,π)|≤LR⋅𝒲1(PMπ(𝒪t+1:T|h),PMπ(𝒪t+1:T|h′)).|\bar{R}(h,\pi)-\bar{R}(h^{\prime},\pi)|\leq L_{R}\cdot\mathcal{W}_{1}\!\bigl(P_{M}^{\pi}(\mathcal{O}_{t+1:T}|h),\,P_{M}^{\pi}(\mathcal{O}_{t+1:T}|h^{\prime})\bigr).

Lemma 46 (Distortion Propagation).

If BB assigns the wrong 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-class at step tt, then 𝒲1​(μ,ν)≤1\mathcal{W}_{1}(\mu,\nu)\leq 1 (discrete metric). If 𝔼⁡[Δt]≤δ\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}]\leq\delta at each step, then |VπA​(M)−VπB​(M)|≤LR⋅T⋅δ|V^{\pi_{A}}(M)-V^{\pi_{B}}(M)|\leq L_{R}\cdot T\cdot\delta.

Proof.

The Wasserstein bound follows from 𝒲1≤∥⋅∥TV≤1\mathcal{W}_{1}\leq\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 1. For propagation: by the value-function error bound of [4] (Theorem: Value-function error bound), |R¯M​(Ht,π)−R¯B​(Ht,π)|≤LR⋅Δt|\bar{R}_{M}(H_{t},\pi)-\bar{R}_{B}(H_{t},\pi)|\leq L_{R}\cdot\Delta_{t}. Summing over TT stages: dval≤LR⋅T⋅dbeh≤LR⋅T⋅δd_{\mathrm{val}}\leq L_{R}\cdot T\cdot d_{\mathrm{beh}}\leq L_{R}\cdot T\cdot\delta. ∎

Proof of Theorem 18(ii).

Step 1 (lossless WZ code above the benchmark). Under the stated assumptions, Corollary 26 identifies the semantic problem exactly with lossless WZ coding on the i.i.d. quotient source, and Corollary 28 gives the lossless benchmark RWZ​(0)=H⁡(QA∣QB)R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(0)=H(Q_{A}\mid Q_{B}). For every rate R>H⁡(QA∣QB)R>H(Q_{A}\mid Q_{B}), the classical WZ/Slepian-Wolf reliability function [29] yields a block code of length TT with reconstruction error probability

Pe(T)≤ 2−T​EWZ​(R)P_{e}^{(T)}\;\leq\;2^{-TE_{\mathrm{WZ}}(R)}

for some exponent EWZ​(R)>0E_{\mathrm{WZ}}(R)>0.

Step 2 (propagation to semantic distortion). On blocks decoded correctly, the induced semantic distortion is zero because the quotient block is reconstructed exactly. On error blocks, the per-step behavioral discrepancy is at most 11, so by Lemma 46 the total semantic distortion over the block is at most LR⋅TL_{R}\cdot T. Therefore

Csem​(R)≤LR⋅T⋅Pe(T)≤LR⋅T⋅2−T​EWZ​(R).∎C_{\mathrm{sem}}(R)\;\leq\;L_{R}\cdot T\cdot P_{e}^{(T)}\;\leq\;L_{R}\cdot T\cdot 2^{-TE_{\mathrm{WZ}}(R)}.\qed

Consistency with parts (i) and (iii).

Part (ii) is intentionally narrower than part (i): it is a constructive theorem only for the one-way i.i.d. benchmark regime. Part (i) remains the structural lower bound outside that regime, and part (iii) still gives perfect alignment by exact quotient transmission when R≥log⁡|𝒬A|R\geq\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|.

Appendix J Proof of Theorem 20: Shrinking-Distortion Converse

Formal setup.

A protocol (E,D)(E,D) consists of encoder Et:(𝒪A)t→MtE_{t}:(\mathcal{O}^{A})^{t}\to M_{t} with H⁡(Mt∣Mt−1)≤RH(M_{t}\mid M^{t-1})\leq R, and bounded decoder D=(πB,U)D=(\pi_{B},U) where πB∈ΠmB,TB\pi_{B}\in\Pi_{m_{B},T_{B}} is an mBm_{B}-node FSC and U:{1,…,2R}→ΘmBU:\{1,\ldots,2^{R}\}\to\Theta_{m_{B}} reconfigures FSC parameters upon each message (see Definition 13). Under Assumption 14, both quotient processes are evaluated on the same source history hth_{t}, so QtA=[ht]mA,TAQ_{t}^{A}=[h_{t}]_{m_{A},T_{A}} and QtB=[ht]mB,TBQ_{t}^{B}=[h_{t}]_{m_{B},T_{B}}. By Assumption 15, the sender intent Intentt=IntentA​(ht)\mathrm{Intent}_{t}=\mathrm{Intent}_{A}(h_{t}) is determined by QtAQ_{t}^{A}, so H⁡(IntentT∣QAT)=0H(\mathrm{Intent}^{T}\mid Q_{A}^{T})=0.

Lemma 47 (Information Bound).

Under Assumptions 14, 19, and 23 and protocol (E,D)(E,D),

I⁡(QAT;MT∣QBT)≤T⋅R.I(Q_{A}^{T};\,M^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})\;\leq\;T\cdot R.
Proof.

Using the chain rule and the rate constraint,

I⁡(QAT;MT∣QBT)≤H⁡(MT∣QBT)≤H⁡(MT)=∑t=1TH⁡(Mt∣Mt−1)≤T​R.∎I(Q_{A}^{T};\,M^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})\;\leq\;H(M^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})\;\leq\;H(M^{T})\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}H(M_{t}\mid M^{t-1})\;\leq\;TR.\qed
Lemma 48 (Semantic Fano Inequality).

Under Assumptions 14, 19, and 23, if a horizon-TT protocol achieves distortion Dintent≤εD_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq\varepsilon with ε′:=2​ε/cM\varepsilon^{\prime}:=2\varepsilon/c_{M} and T​ε′≤1/2T\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq 1/2, then

1T​H​(QAT∣MT,QBT)≤h⁡(ε′)+ε′​log|𝒬A|+oT​(1).\frac{1}{T}H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid M^{T},Q_{B}^{T})\;\leq\;h(\varepsilon^{\prime})+\varepsilon^{\prime}\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|+o_{T}(1).

Regime restriction. The block error probability Pe(block)≤T​ε′P_{e}^{(\mathrm{block})}\leq T\varepsilon^{\prime} from the union bound requires T​ε′≤1/2T\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq 1/2 for Fano’s inequality to be non-vacuous, i.e., ε≤cM/(4​T)\varepsilon\leq c_{M}/(4T). This restriction grows tighter with horizon TT. Consequently, the converse (Theorem 20) is formally operative only in the regime ε=O⁡(1/T)\varepsilon=O(1/T). As in Remark 21, we separate empirical roles: Figure 2 uses fixed ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1 to illustrate the structural phase transition (Theorem 18)—not the converse—while Figure 3 runs εT=0.4/T\varepsilon_{T}=0.4/T over varying TT, matching the shrinking-distortion scaling class of this lemma. Neither figure should be read as a pointwise empirical proof of the converse bound; the asymptotic form (T→∞T\to\infty with ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 at rate O⁡(1/T)O(1/T)) remains the formally justified regime. See Appendix M for protocol details.

Proof.

Let YT:=(MT,QBT)Y^{T}:=(M^{T},Q_{B}^{T}) denote the full decoder-side information. For each step tt, define Q^t=gt​(YT)\hat{Q}_{t}=g_{t}(Y^{T}) as the nearest-intent decoder: among the reachable 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses consistent with the observed 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-class, choose the one whose induced sender intent is closest (under dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}}) to the receiver intent realized by the protocol. Because distinct merged 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses are separated by at least cMc_{M}, a nearest-neighbor error implies the realized per-step distortion is at least cM/2c_{M}/2. Therefore, with Zt:=𝟏{Q^t≠QtA}Z_{t}:=\mathbf{1}\{\hat{Q}_{t}\neq Q_{t}^{A}\},

ε≥Dintent=1T∑t=1T𝔼[dintent,t]≥cM2⋅1T∑t=1Tℙ(Zt=1),\varepsilon\;\geq\;D_{\mathrm{intent}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[d_{\mathrm{intent},t}]\;\geq\;\frac{c_{M}}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{P}(Z_{t}=1),

giving the average per-step error probability P¯e:=1T​∑tℙ⁡(Zt=1)≤2​ε/cM=:ε′\bar{P}_{e}:=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\mathbb{P}(Z_{t}=1)\leq 2\varepsilon/c_{M}=:\varepsilon^{\prime}.

Per-step to block conversion. Choose blocklength nT:=⌊T⌋n_{T}:=\lfloor\sqrt{T}\rfloor. Write T=BT​nT+rTT=B_{T}n_{T}+r_{T} with BT:=⌊T/nT⌋B_{T}:=\lfloor T/n_{T}\rfloor full blocks and remainder 0≤rT<nT0\leq r_{T}<n_{T}. For each full block bb, let QA,bnTQ_{A,b}^{n_{T}} be the corresponding length-nTn_{T} substring of QATQ_{A}^{T}, and let Q^A,bnT\hat{Q}_{A,b}^{n_{T}} be its MAP estimate from YTY^{T}. Since the average per-step error probability satisfies P¯e≤ε′\bar{P}_{e}\leq\varepsilon^{\prime}, a union bound over the nTn_{T} symbols in block bb gives

ℙ⁡(QA,bnT≠Q^A,bnT)≤nT​ε′.\mathbb{P}\!\bigl(Q_{A,b}^{n_{T}}\neq\hat{Q}_{A,b}^{n_{T}}\bigr)\;\leq\;n_{T}\varepsilon^{\prime}.

Because T​ε′≤1/2T\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq 1/2, we have nT​ε′≤T​ε′≤1/(2​T)n_{T}\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq\sqrt{T}\,\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq 1/(2\sqrt{T}), so Fano’s inequality is eventually non-vacuous on every full block. Applying the |𝒬A|nT|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|^{n_{T}}-ary Fano bound to block bb yields

1nT​H​(QA,bnT∣YT)≤1nT​h​(nT​ε′)+ε′⋅1nT​log⁡(|𝒬A|nT−1).\frac{1}{n_{T}}H(Q_{A,b}^{n_{T}}\mid Y^{T})\;\leq\;\frac{1}{n_{T}}h(n_{T}\varepsilon^{\prime})+\varepsilon^{\prime}\cdot\frac{1}{n_{T}}\log(|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|^{n_{T}}-1).

Using the block chain rule and bounding the remainder by rT​log⁡|𝒬A|r_{T}\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|,

1T​H​(QAT∣YT)≤BTT​h​(nT​ε′)+BT​nTT​ε′⋅1nT​log⁡(|𝒬A|nT−1)+rTT​log⁡|𝒬A|.\frac{1}{T}H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid Y^{T})\;\leq\;\frac{B_{T}}{T}h(n_{T}\varepsilon^{\prime})\;+\;\frac{B_{T}n_{T}}{T}\,\varepsilon^{\prime}\cdot\frac{1}{n_{T}}\log(|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|^{n_{T}}-1)\;+\;\frac{r_{T}}{T}\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|.

Now nT→∞n_{T}\to\infty, rT/T→0r_{T}/T\to 0, and nT​ε′≤1/(2​T)→0n_{T}\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq 1/(2\sqrt{T})\to 0, so BTT​h​(nT​ε′)=oT​(1)\frac{B_{T}}{T}h(n_{T}\varepsilon^{\prime})=o_{T}(1) and

1nT​log⁡(|𝒬A|nT−1)=log⁡|𝒬A|+oT​(1).\frac{1}{n_{T}}\log(|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|^{n_{T}}-1)=\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|+o_{T}(1).

Therefore

1T​H​(QAT∣MT,QBT)≤ε′​log⁡|𝒬A|+oT​(1)≤h⁡(ε′)+ε′​log|𝒬A|+oT​(1).∎\frac{1}{T}H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid M^{T},Q_{B}^{T})\;\leq\;\varepsilon^{\prime}\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|+o_{T}(1)\;\leq\;h(\varepsilon^{\prime})+\varepsilon^{\prime}\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|+o_{T}(1).\qed
Proof of Theorem 20.

Setup. Fix horizon TT and protocol (E(T),D(T))(E^{(T)},D^{(T)}) with per-step rate RTR_{T} and distortion εT\varepsilon_{T}; write εT′:=2​εT/cM\varepsilon_{T}^{\prime}:=2\varepsilon_{T}/c_{M}.

Step 1. Since QBTQ_{B}^{T} is decoder side information and the messages are the only communicated bits, decompose:

I⁡(QAT;MT∣QBT)=H⁡(QAT∣QBT)−H⁡(QAT∣MT,QBT).I(Q_{A}^{T};\,M^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})=H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})-H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid M^{T},Q_{B}^{T}).

Step 2. Since 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} refines 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}, knowing QATQ_{A}^{T} determines QBTQ_{B}^{T}, so I⁡(QAT,QBT)=H⁡(QBT)I(Q_{A}^{T};Q_{B}^{T})=H(Q_{B}^{T}). Therefore:

H⁡(QAT∣QBT)=H⁡(QAT)−H⁡(QBT).H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})=H(Q_{A}^{T})-H(Q_{B}^{T}).

By Assumption 19, the quotient processes are stationary ergodic with entropy rates hA,hBh_{A},h_{B} (Remark 43): H⁡(QAT)=T​hA+o⁡(T)H(Q_{A}^{T})=Th_{A}+o(T) and H⁡(QBT)=T​hB+o⁡(T)H(Q_{B}^{T})=Th_{B}+o(T). Hence H⁡(QAT∣QBT)=T⁡(hA−hB)+o⁡(T)H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})=T(h_{A}-h_{B})+o(T).

Step 3. By Lemma 48: H⁡(QAT∣MT,QBT)≤T⋅h⁡(εT′)+εT′⋅T​log|𝒬A|+o⁡(T)H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid M^{T},Q_{B}^{T})\leq T\cdot h(\varepsilon_{T}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{T}^{\prime}\cdot T\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|+o(T).

Step 4. By Lemma 47: T⋅RT≥I⁡(QAT;MT∣QBT)T\cdot R_{T}\geq I(Q_{A}^{T};\,M^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T}).

Step 5. Combining Steps 1–4 and dividing by TT gives

RT≥(hA−hB)−h⁡(εT′)−εT′​log⁡|𝒬A|−oT​(1).R_{T}\;\geq\;(h_{A}-h_{B})-h(\varepsilon_{T}^{\prime})-\varepsilon_{T}^{\prime}\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|-o_{T}(1).

If εT′→0\varepsilon_{T}^{\prime}\to 0, taking lim infT→∞\liminf_{T\to\infty} yields lim infTRT≥hA−hB\liminf_{T}R_{T}\geq h_{A}-h_{B}. Under near-uniform quotient distributions (hA≈log⁡|𝒬A|h_{A}\approx\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|, hB≈log⁡|𝒬B|h_{B}\approx\log|\mathcal{Q}_{B}|; see Remark 43), this recovers the log-cardinality reference. The one-way WZ reduction (Proposition 25) sharpens the converse at D=0D=0 to the benchmark R≥RWZ​(0)=H⁡(QA∣QB)R\geq R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(0)=H(Q_{A}\mid Q_{B}); the matching achievability direction is exact only for i.i.d. sources and otherwise argued separately in Section 7. ∎

Remark 49 (Decoder-side interpretation).

The theorem does not require an additional slack parameter. If one nevertheless wants to compare the converse bound to the information actually extracted from messages, the natural quantity is the residual uncertainty

1T​H​(QAT∣MT,QBT)=1T​H​(QAT∣QBT)−1T​I​(QAT;MT∣QBT).\frac{1}{T}H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid M^{T},Q_{B}^{T})\;=\;\frac{1}{T}H(Q_{A}^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})-\frac{1}{T}I(Q_{A}^{T};\,M^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T}).

Under Assumption 19, this equals (hA−hB)−1T​I​(QAT;MT∣QBT)+oT​(1)(h_{A}-h_{B})-\frac{1}{T}I(Q_{A}^{T};\,M^{T}\mid Q_{B}^{T})+o_{T}(1), so it measures how far the received messages fall short of saturating the conditional entropy rate available beyond QBTQ_{B}^{T}. At the lossless one-way WZ benchmark, this residual vanishes asymptotically.

Appendix K Proof of Theorem 31: Alignment Traversal

Proof.

For any [h]A∈𝒬A[h]_{A}\in\mathcal{Q}_{A}, write φ=φk−1∘⋯∘φ1\varphi=\varphi_{k-1}\circ\cdots\circ\varphi_{1} and apply the triangle inequality for 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}:

𝒲1(PM(⋅|[h]A),PM(⋅|φ([h]A)))\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{1}\!\bigl(P_{M}(\cdot|[h]_{A}),\,P_{M}(\cdot|\varphi([h]_{A}))\bigr) ≤∑i=1k−1𝒲1(PM(⋅|φi−1:1([h]A)),PM(⋅|φi:1([h]A)))\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathcal{W}_{1}\!\bigl(P_{M}(\cdot|\varphi_{i-1:1}([h]_{A})),\,P_{M}(\cdot|\varphi_{i:1}([h]_{A}))\bigr)
≤∑i=1k−1Li⋅dQ​(Πi,Πi+1∣M),\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}L_{i}\cdot d_{Q}(\Pi_{i},\Pi_{i+1}\mid M),

where φi:1:=φi∘⋯∘φ1\varphi_{i:1}:=\varphi_{i}\circ\cdots\circ\varphi_{1} and the second inequality uses the LiL_{i}-Lipschitz property of each φi\varphi_{i}. Taking the supremum over [h]A[h]_{A} yields dQ​(A,B∣M)≤∑iLi⋅dQ​(Πi,Πi+1∣M)d_{Q}(A,B\mid M)\leq\sum_{i}L_{i}\cdot d_{Q}(\Pi_{i},\Pi_{i+1}\mid M).

For the rate statement, fix protocols for each adjacent pair (Πi,Πi+1)(\Pi_{i},\Pi_{i+1}) achieving distortion at most ε/k\varepsilon/k with rates arbitrarily close to Rsem(Πi→Πi+1;ε/k)R_{\mathrm{sem}}(\Pi_{i}\to\Pi_{i+1};\,\varepsilon/k). Compose these protocols sequentially through the intermediate agents. The total rate is the sum of the stage rates, and the total distortion is at most ε\varepsilon by the triangle inequality / budget split. Taking infima over the stage protocols gives

Rsem(A→B;ε)≤∑iRsem(Πi→Πi+1;ε/k),R_{\mathrm{sem}}(A\to B;\,\varepsilon)\leq\sum_{i}R_{\mathrm{sem}}(\Pi_{i}\to\Pi_{i+1};\,\varepsilon/k),

which is exactly the claimed traversal bound. ∎

Appendix L Codebook Performance Bound

Theorem 50 (Codebook Performance, restated).

The semantic codebook of Definition 34 achieves Dintent≤O(|𝒬A|1/d⋅2−R/d)D_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq O(|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|^{1/d}\cdot 2^{-R/d}), where dd is the effective dimension of the intent space.

Proof.

The 2R2^{R} codewords partition the |𝒬A||\mathcal{Q}_{A}| quotient classes into K=2RK=2^{R} Voronoi cells in the dd-dimensional intent space. By standard kk-means quantization theory [18], 𝔼⁡[‖I−I^‖]≤Cd⋅(|𝒬A|/K)1/d\mathbb{E}[\|I-\hat{I}\|]\leq C_{d}\cdot(|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|/K)^{1/d} for a dd-dimensional uniform source, where CdC_{d} depends only on dimension. Substituting K=2RK=2^{R} and using dintent≤‖I−I^‖1d_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq\|I-\hat{I}\|_{1} (since each component of dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}}—belief 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}, policy TV, value difference—is bounded by the corresponding L1L_{1} component of the intent vector difference under ‖R‖∞≤1\|R\|_{\infty}\leq 1) gives the bound. For Markovian priors, the same construction remains a valid memoryless encoder and therefore provides a conservative constructive upper bound; allowing encoders with memory can only improve on it. ∎

Appendix M Additional Experimental Details

Environments.

Tiger [8]: A two-door problem where the agent must determine which door hides a tiger based on noisy observations. We used T=4T=4, mA=3m_{A}=3, mB=1m_{B}=1. The quotient computation yielded |𝒬A|=31|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|=31 and |𝒬B|=15|\mathcal{Q}_{B}|=15 classes, giving Rcrit≈1.05R_{\mathrm{crit}}\approx 1.05 bits/step. Below RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}}, distortion remains above 0.30.3; above RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}}, it decays rapidly toward zero, reaching Dintent<0.02D_{\mathrm{intent}}<0.02 at R=3R=3 bits/step (see Figure 9). At R≥log⁡|𝒬A|≈4.95R\geq\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|\approx 4.95 bits/step, perfect alignment is achieved (Dintent=0D_{\mathrm{intent}}=0), confirming Theorem 18(iii).

Chain5: A 5-state chain POMDP (|S|=5|S|\!=\!5, |A|=2|A|\!=\!2, |O|=5|O|\!=\!5, obs. noise 0.30.3) designed to produce large quotient gaps. The main experiments use T=4T=4 with mA=16m_{A}=16 and mB∈{1,2,4,8}m_{B}\in\{1,2,4,8\}. For mB=1m_{B}=1: |𝒬A|=781|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|=781, |𝒬B|=289|\mathcal{Q}_{B}|=289, giving Rcritlog=log⁡(781/289)≈1.43R_{\mathrm{crit}}^{\log}=\log(781/289)\approx 1.43 bits/step. The large quotient gap produces a sharp phase transition in the rate-distortion curve (Figure 2).

Codebook construction.

For each rate R∈{0,0.5,…,7}R\in\{0,0.5,\ldots,7\} bits/step, we ran 1010 independent trials with different random seeds for FSC sampling and codebook construction. We report the median intent distortion; shaded regions in figures indicate the interquartile range (25th–75th percentile). Semantic codebooks use Definition 34, constructing quotient-aware partitions and measuring operational DintentD_{\mathrm{intent}}. Classical baselines are Shannon-theoretic reference curves, not operational coding schemes: observation compression uses D=max⁡(0,(H⁡(O)−R)/H⁡(O))D=\max(0,\,(H(O)-R)/H(O)), and belief compression uses D=max⁡(0,(H⁡(B)−R)/H⁡(B))D=\max(0,\,(H(B)-R)/H(B)), where H⁡(O)H(O) and H⁡(B)H(B) are the marginal entropy of the observation and belief processes respectively.

Intent distortion measurement.

Experiments use the two-term proxy dintentexp(h):=∥bhA−bhB∥1+0.5⋅𝟏{aA≠aB}d_{\mathrm{intent}}^{\mathrm{exp}}(h):=\|b_{h}^{A}-b_{h}^{B}\|_{1}+0.5\cdot\mathbf{1}\{a_{A}\neq a_{B}\}, omitting the value-difference term from the full three-term dintentd_{\mathrm{intent}} (Remark 10). By Proposition 11, dintentexp≤dintent≤dintentexp+|VπA​(h)−VπB​(h)|d_{\mathrm{intent}}^{\mathrm{exp}}\leq d_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq d_{\mathrm{intent}}^{\mathrm{exp}}+|V^{\pi_{A}}(h)-V^{\pi_{B}}(h)|: the proxy is a lower bound on the full measure, and the phase transition location and exponential exponent are invariant to this choice (they depend on quotient entropy, not distortion scale). On Chain5 with LR≈0.74L_{R}\approx 0.74 and maxh⁡dbeh​(h)≤1\max_{h}d_{\mathrm{beh}}(h)\leq 1 (Wasserstein distance bounded by 1 under the discrete observation metric), the value-difference gap is bounded by LR⋅T⋅maxh⁡dbeh​(h)≤0.74⋅5⋅1=3.7L_{R}\cdot T\cdot\max_{h}d_{\mathrm{beh}}(h)\leq 0.74\cdot 5\cdot 1=3.7, so the two measures agree qualitatively. We measured DintentexpD_{\mathrm{intent}}^{\mathrm{exp}} by sampling 10,00010{,}000 trajectories under each policy and computing the empirical average.

Alignment scaling sweep.

For Figure 2, we generated 1212 POMDP instances with varying state/observation sizes and computed quotients at multiple memory levels (mA,mB)(m_{A},m_{B}). For each configuration, we performed binary search on RR to find RminR_{\min} achieving Dintent≤0.1D_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq 0.1.

Shrinking-distortion sweep.

To match the regime of the asymptotic one-way converse, we ran a dedicated Chain5 sweep at (mA,mB)=(16,1)(m_{A},m_{B})=(16,1) with horizons T∈{2,3,4,5}T\in\{2,3,4,5\} and threshold εT=0.4/T\varepsilon_{T}=0.4/T. For each horizon we recomputed (𝒬A,𝒬B)(\mathcal{Q}_{A},\mathcal{Q}_{B}) and searched integer rates R∈{0,…,12}R\in\{0,\ldots,12\} for the first rate achieving Dintent≤εTD_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq\varepsilon_{T}. The resulting thresholds were Rmin=5,8,10,12R_{\min}=5,8,10,12, while the corresponding log-cardinality references were 0.43,0.79,1.43,2.290.43,0.79,1.43,2.29 bits/step. We use this sweep as a regime-matching illustration for Theorem 20, not as a pointwise empirical proof of the converse itself.

Quotient computation algorithm.

The quotient 𝒬A=Qm,T​(M)\mathcal{Q}_{A}=Q_{m,T}(M) is computed as follows: (1) FSC generation: for m≤3m\leq 3, enumerate all deterministic mm-node FSCs; for m>3m>3, sample nFSCn_{\mathrm{FSC}} random stochastic FSCs uniformly (nFSC=80n_{\mathrm{FSC}}=80 for the main Chain5 experiments; 5050 for RichGridWorld and BalancedRand8). (2) Signature computation: for each history h∈𝒪≤Th\in\mathcal{O}^{\leq T} and each FSC π\pi, compute the future observation distribution PMπ​(Ot+1∣h)P_{M}^{\pi}(O_{t+1}\mid h); the behavioral signature of hh is the tuple of these distributions across all FSCs. (3) Equivalence grouping: histories with identical signatures (to numerical tolerance 10−410^{-4}) form equivalence classes; the number of distinct classes is |𝒬A||\mathcal{Q}_{A}|. Enumeration is exponential in mm; sampling is polynomial per FSC but requires sufficient samples for accurate quotient estimation. In our experiments, nFSC≥50n_{\mathrm{FSC}}\geq 50 suffices for m≤16m\leq 16 with |𝒪|≤5|\mathcal{O}|\leq 5 (convergence validated in Figure 11).

Quotient estimation convergence.

To validate that random FSC sampling produces stable quotient estimates, we swept nFSC∈{5,10,20,30,50,80,100,150,200}n_{\mathrm{FSC}}\in\{5,10,20,30,50,80,100,150,200\} for Chain5 at m∈{1,2,4}m\in\{1,2,4\} with 10 seeds each (Figure 11). For m=1m=1, full enumeration is feasible and |𝒬||\mathcal{Q}| is constant at 289. For m=2m=2, the estimate rises from 688 (nFSC=5n_{\mathrm{FSC}}=5) to 774 by nFSC=20n_{\mathrm{FSC}}=20 and stabilizes. For m=4m=4, stabilization to 781 occurs by nFSC=10n_{\mathrm{FSC}}=10. The IQR bands vanish by nFSC=20n_{\mathrm{FSC}}=20, confirming that moderate sampling suffices.

Proposition 51 (Quotient estimation sample complexity).

Let MM be a POMDP with |𝒪||\mathcal{O}| observations and horizon TT, and let the true quotient Qm,T​(M)Q_{m,T}(M) have separation margin γ:=minh≢h′⁡‖sig⁡(h)−sig⁡(h′)‖1>0\gamma:=\min_{h\not\equiv h^{\prime}}\|\mathrm{sig}(h)-\mathrm{sig}(h^{\prime})\|_{1}>0, where sig⁡(h)\mathrm{sig}(h) concatenates the one-step future distributions across all mm-node FSCs. If nn FSCs are sampled i.i.d. uniformly from the set of all |𝒜|m⋅mm​|𝒪||\mathcal{A}|^{m}\cdot m^{m|\mathcal{O}|} deterministic mm-node FSCs, then with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta over the sample, the estimated quotient partition equals the true partition, provided

n≥1pγ​(2​T​log⁡|𝒪|+log⁡(1/δ)),n\;\geq\;\frac{1}{p_{\gamma}}\,\bigl(2T\log|\mathcal{O}|+\log(1/\delta)\bigr), (2)

where pγ:=minh≢h′Prπ∼Unif[∥sigπ(h)−sigπ(h′)∥1>γ/2]p_{\gamma}:=\min_{h\not\equiv h^{\prime}}\,\Pr_{\pi\sim\mathrm{Unif}}[\|\mathrm{sig}_{\pi}(h)-\mathrm{sig}_{\pi}(h^{\prime})\|_{1}>\gamma/2] is the minimum per-FSC distinguishing probability.

Proof sketch.

For each inequivalent pair (h,h′)(h,h^{\prime}), a uniformly random FSC distinguishes them with probability ≥pγ\geq p_{\gamma}. With nn i.i.d. samples, the probability that no sample separates the pair is (1−pγ)n≤e−n​pγ(1-p_{\gamma})^{n}\leq e^{-np_{\gamma}}. The number of history pairs is at most |𝒪|2​T|\mathcal{O}|^{2T}; a union bound gives Pr⁡[any pair missed]≤|𝒪|2​T⋅e−n​pγ\Pr[\text{any pair missed}]\leq|\mathcal{O}|^{2T}\cdot e^{-np_{\gamma}}. Setting this ≤δ\leq\delta and solving yields (2). ∎

Remark 52 (Practical implications).

In the worst case, pγ≥1/NFSCp_{\gamma}\geq 1/N_{\mathrm{FSC}} where NFSC=|𝒜|m⋅mm​|𝒪|N_{\mathrm{FSC}}=|\mathcal{A}|^{m}\cdot m^{m|\mathcal{O}|}, making nn exponential in mm—consistent with the NEXP-completeness of Dec-POMDP planning [25]. In practice, pγp_{\gamma} is much larger: our convergence experiments (Figure 11) show stabilisation at n≈20n\approx 20 for m≤16m\leq 16 with |𝒪|=5|\mathcal{O}|=5, suggesting pγ≫1/NFSCp_{\gamma}\gg 1/N_{\mathrm{FSC}} for structured POMDPs.

Assumption verification on Chain5.

We computed the refinement ratio for (mA=16,mB=1)(m_{A}=16,\,m_{B}=1) on Chain5: |𝒬A|=781|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|=781, |𝒬B|=289|\mathcal{Q}_{B}|=289, r¯=2.70\bar{r}=2.70, maxk⁡rk=43\max_{k}r_{k}=43, giving ratio maxk⁡rk/r¯=15.9\max_{k}r_{k}/\bar{r}=15.9. The refinement is notably non-uniform: some 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B}-classes contain up to 43 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}-subclasses. This is precisely why we do not use Chain5 as validation of a sharp theorem-level constructive exponent; we use it instead as structural and benchmark evidence. The observation-Lipschitz constant was estimated at LR≈0.74L_{R}\approx 0.74, confirming the Lipschitz reward structure holds with a moderate constant.

Quotient entropies and one-way critical-rate benchmark.

We estimated marginal quotient entropies via 10,000 simulated trajectories of length 50 on Chain5, mapping beliefs to quotient classes at each step. For (mA=16,mB=1)(m_{A}=16,\,m_{B}=1): H⁡(QA)≈6.03H(Q_{A})\approx 6.03 bits vs. log⁡|𝒬A|=9.61\log|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|=9.61, and H⁡(QB)≈5.44H(Q_{B})\approx 5.44 bits vs. log⁡|𝒬B|=8.17\log|\mathcal{Q}_{B}|=8.17—marginal entropies at only 63% and 67% of their maxima. Since 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B} coarsens 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A}, the i.i.d. critical rate is H⁡(QA)−H⁡(QB)≈0.59H(Q_{A})-H(Q_{B})\approx 0.59 bits/step, which is 59%59\% below the log-cardinality approximation of 1.431.43. This confirms non-uniform quotient distributions significantly lower the one-way WZ benchmark relative to the log-cardinality approximation.

Per-step conditional entropy rates estimated independently were H⁡(QAt∣QAt−1)≈2.39H(Q_{A}^{t}\mid Q_{A}^{t-1})\approx 2.39 and H⁡(QBt∣QBt−1)≈2.45H(Q_{B}^{t}\mid Q_{B}^{t-1})\approx 2.45, indicating substantial temporal correlation. The marginal difference hA−hB≈−0.05h_{A}-h_{B}\approx-0.05 is an artifact of computing the rates from separate trajectory ensembles: the L1-distance belief classification introduces small errors that break the exact coarsening property.

Effective intent dimension (codebook bound validation).

The codebook performance bound (Appendix L) depends on the effective dimension dd of the intent space. For Chain5 (|S|=5|S|=5), PCA on the 781 quotient-class belief centroids yields: 2 components explain 87% of variance, 3 explain 95%, and all 4 non-degenerate components explain 100%. Thus deff=4d_{\mathrm{eff}}=4 (matching |S|−1|S|-1, the simplex dimension). The codebook bound predicts Dintent≤O(7811/4⋅2−R/4)≈O(5.3⋅2−R/4)D_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq O(781^{1/4}\cdot 2^{-R/4})\approx O(5.3\cdot 2^{-R/4}), consistent with the empirical decay observed in Figure 2.

Blahut-Arimoto RWZ​(D)R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D) computation.

To compare the experiments against the WZ benchmark (Proposition 25) numerically, we compute the i.i.d. quantity RWZ​(D)R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D) on Chain5’s quotient alphabets via the standard alternating minimization [35]: given source distribution p⁡(qA)p(q_{A}) (estimated from 2,0002{,}000 trajectories), distortion matrix dintent​(qAi,qAj)d_{\mathrm{intent}}(q_{A}^{i},q_{A}^{j}) over all |𝒬A|2|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|^{2} pairs, and deterministic coarsening f:𝒬A→𝒬Bf\!:\mathcal{Q}_{A}\!\to\!\mathcal{Q}_{B}, the WZ iteration alternates

q⁡(u∣x)∝p⁡(u∣y=f⁡(x))​e−s​d​(x,u),p⁡(u∣y)=∑xp⁡(x∣y)​q​(u∣x),q(u\mid x)\;\propto\;p(u\mid y\!=\!f(x))\,e^{-s\,d(x,u)},\qquad p(u\mid y)=\sum_{x}p(x\mid y)\,q(u\mid x),

with Lagrange parameter ss swept over [0.01, 316][0.01,\,316] on a log-spaced grid (32 points). We also compute the standard R⁡(D)R(D) (no side information) by replacing p⁡(u∣y)p(u\mid y) with p⁡(u)p(u). Filtering to the 234234 visited quotient classes, H⁡(QA∣QB)=0.29H(Q_{A}\mid Q_{B})=0.29 bits under the i.i.d. marginal, consistent with the computed RWZ​(0)≈0.29R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(0)\approx 0.29 bits. The gap R​(D)−RWZ​(D)R(D)-R_{\mathrm{WZ}}(D) measures the value of B’s side information.

Balanced-refinement environment.

BalancedRand8 is a random POMDP (|S|=8|S|\!=\!8, |A|=2|A|\!=\!2, |O|=2|O|\!=\!2, seed 8) selected from 2,0002{,}000 random POMDPs with 44 memory/horizon configurations each, targeting uniform refinement ratio <3<3 with capacity gap >0.5>0.5 bits. The selected instance has mA=4m_{A}\!=\!4, T=4T\!=\!4, |𝒬A|=31|\mathcal{Q}_{A}|\!=\!31, |𝒬B|=10|\mathcal{Q}_{B}|\!=\!10 (for mB=1m_{B}\!=\!1), refinement ratio 2.582.58, and Rcrit≈1.63R_{\mathrm{crit}}\approx 1.63 bits/step. The refinement distribution rk=[8,6,5,5,2,1,1,1,1,1]r_{k}=[8,6,5,5,2,1,1,1,1,1] is substantially more uniform than Chain5’s (rk=[43,43,…]r_{k}=[43,43,\ldots], ratio 15.915.9). Baseline coding comparisons.

For k-means baseline, we cluster the |𝒬A||\mathcal{Q}_{A}| belief centroids using kk-means in L1L_{1} geometry with kk-means++ initialization at each rate level R∈{0,1,…,10}R\in\{0,1,\ldots,10\}. Each cluster maps to the nearest 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B} class, and DintentD_{\mathrm{intent}} is computed as the p⁡(qA)p(q_{A})-weighted average intent distortion. Random clustering averages 55 trials of uniform random label assignment. The comparison confirms that quotient-aware clustering outperforms geometry-only clustering (k-means) and random clustering at all rates, with the gap widest at intermediate rates near RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}}.

Appendix N Continuous Spaces Extension

Proposition 53 (Continuous Semantic Rate-Distortion Bound).

Let 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} and 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B} be quotient spaces with metric dd and ε\varepsilon-covering numbers N⁡(ε,𝒬A,d)N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q}_{A},d) and N⁡(ε,𝒬B,d)N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q}_{B},d). Then any protocol achieving Dintent≤εD_{\mathrm{intent}}\leq\varepsilon requires:

R≥log⁡N⁡(ε,𝒬A,d)−log⁡N⁡(ε,𝒬B,d)−h⁡(ε′)−ε′​log⁡N⁡(ε,𝒬A,d).R\;\geq\;\log N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q}_{A},d)-\log N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q}_{B},d)-h(\varepsilon^{\prime})-\varepsilon^{\prime}\log N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q}_{A},d).

For smooth quotient manifolds of intrinsic dimensions dAd_{A} and dBd_{B}: log⁡N⁡(ε,𝒬,d)≈d⋅log⁡(1/ε)+O⁡(1)\log N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q},d)\approx d\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)+O(1), yielding R≥(dA−dB)​log⁡(1/ε)−O⁡(ε)R\geq(d_{A}-d_{B})\log(1/\varepsilon)-O(\varepsilon).

Proof sketch.

Replace |𝒬||\mathcal{Q}| with N⁡(ε,𝒬,d)N(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q},d) in the Fano argument (Appendix J). Each ε\varepsilon-ball in 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} mapping to the same ε\varepsilon-ball in 𝒬B\mathcal{Q}_{B} constitutes an ambiguity cell of the same structure as the discrete case. ∎

Appendix P LLM Routing as Semantic Communication (Analogical Case Study)

This appendix presents an analogical illustration—not a formal instantiation—of the framework’s qualitative predictions in a practical LLM setting. The LLM representations are not quotient POMDPs; the value of the case study is that it exhibits the same qualitative phenomena (phase transition, probe-family dependence) that the theory predicts.

To that end, we analyze LLM model routing as an instance of semantic communication. A strong model (GPT-4) is selectively invoked based on a weak model’s (Mixtral-8x7B) self-assessment—a 1-bit communication protocol at rate R=1R=1 bit/query.

Phase transition via probe family richness.

We report APGR (Accuracy Per GPU-hour Ratio): APGR :⁣=:= (accuracy of routing policy) / (mean GPU-hours per query under routing policy), normalized so that APGR =1=1 corresponds to always using the strong model at its accuracy ceiling. Higher APGR indicates better accuracy-efficiency tradeoff [19]. On MMLU [20] (14K questions, 69% weak accuracy), single-token logprobs achieve APGR =0.620=0.620, outperforming embedding-based routing (0.5180.518). On the harder MMLU-Pro [21] (12K questions, 33% weak accuracy), logprobs fail (APGR =0.457=0.457, below random at 0.5020.502): the competence band is exceeded.

Richer probe recovers signal.

Self-consistency sampling [14] (N=8N=8 completions) achieves APGR =2.216=2.216 on MMLU-Pro, a 36% improvement. This confirms the theory: ΠSC\Pi_{\text{SC}} is a richer probe family, yielding a finer quotient |Q⁡(ΠSC)|>|Q⁡(Πlogprob)||Q(\Pi_{\text{SC}})|>|Q(\Pi_{\text{logprob}})|. At the 90% quality threshold, the router saves 28% of inference cost.

Interpretation.

The routing problem instantiates semantic communication: the weak model’s uncertainty signal is a quotient-aware code, and the router’s boundary corresponds to RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}}. We emphasize this is an analogy grounded in the framework’s structure, not a formal deduction—the LLM’s representations are not quotient POMDPs. The analogy is useful because it predicts the qualitative phenomena (phase transition, probe family dependence) observed empirically.

Appendix Q Lattice-Gradient Quotient Estimation

The worst-case complexity of absolute quotient estimation is exponential in mm (Proposition 51). We outline a differential approach that avoids this barrier by exploiting the lattice structure of the quotient functor QQ.

Core idea.

The refinement lemma (Lemma 39) orders quotients by capacity: m<m′m<m^{\prime} implies 𝒬m\mathcal{Q}_{m} coarsens 𝒬m′\mathcal{Q}_{m^{\prime}}. Instead of computing 𝒬m\mathcal{Q}_{m} from scratch at target capacity mm, enter the lattice at a small computable capacity m0m_{0} (where enumeration is tractable) and estimate the differential refinement Δ​Qk→k+1\Delta Q_{k\to k+1}—the additional distinctions gained by moving from capacity kk to k+1k+1—at each step along the chain m0,m0+1,…,mm_{0},m_{0}{+}1,\ldots,m.

Lipschitz chaining.

By Theorem 31, the alignment rate between adjacent levels satisfies Rsem(Πk→Πk+1;ε)≤Lk⋅∥ΔQk→k+1∥R_{\mathrm{sem}}(\Pi_{k}\to\Pi_{k+1};\varepsilon)\leq L_{k}\cdot\|\Delta Q_{k\to k+1}\|, where LkL_{k} is the local Lipschitz constant of the quotient morphism. Summing: the total error from chaining m−m0m-m_{0} local estimates accumulates linearly, not exponentially, in the capacity gap. Each local Δ​Q\Delta Q estimate requires only a polynomial number of cross-probes—input pairs that are equivalent at level kk but distinguished at level k+1k{+}1—whose count is bounded by |𝒬k+1|−|𝒬k||\mathcal{Q}_{k+1}|-|\mathcal{Q}_{k}|.

Language as probe family.

For language-based agents, the self-referential closure of natural language provides a scalable probe family without FSC enumeration. A linguistic cross-probe is a prompt pair (p,p′)(p,p^{\prime}) designed so that a capacity-kk model responds identically but a capacity-(k+1)(k{+}1) model distinguishes them (e.g., paraphrases that require deeper contextual reasoning to separate). Neural representation clusters at intermediate layers provide empirical proxies for quotient class membership, connecting Δ​Q\Delta Q estimation to standard probing methodology in interpretability research.

Open conjectures.

  1. 1.

    Bridge: Neural representation clusters at layer ll of a transformer refine the Myhill–Nerode quotient 𝒬m,T​(M)\mathcal{Q}_{m,T}(M) for an effective capacity m⁡(l)m(l) determined by the layer’s representational bandwidth.

  2. 2.

    Smoothness: The quotient lattice for language-based agents is connected and locally smooth—adjacent capacity levels produce O⁡(1)O(1) new quotient classes per step, making the chaining error well-controlled.

These conjectures are empirically testable via layer-wise probing of language models at varying scales, and if confirmed, would make RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}} estimation polynomial in mm for practical architectures.

Broader Impact

This work provides information-theoretic tools for quantifying alignment costs between agents of different computational capacities. The framework’s primary intended application is understanding and improving human–AI alignment: quantifying the minimum feedback bandwidth for safe AI behavior and identifying when alignment is structurally impossible given capacity constraints. This has positive implications for the principled design of RLHF pipelines and interpretability methods.

However, the framework also reveals fundamental limits. The structural impossibility below RcritR_{\mathrm{crit}} implies that some agent pairs cannot be aligned regardless of communication protocol design. If misinterpreted, this could discourage alignment efforts in regimes where they are most needed. We emphasize that the impossibility is rate-limited, not absolute: increasing the communication rate (e.g., richer feedback mechanisms) can always reduce the gap. The framework should be used to design better alignment protocols, not to justify inadequate ones.
